divorce noun and verb

also get a divorce, divorced, get divorced, separate (of a married couple), seek a divorce, divorce someone

classical

Cic. Att. 13.7.1: Lentulum cum Metellā certē fēcisse dīvortium (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 194, 305
M-O s.v. divorce (vb.)
Traupman 194

dīvortium, dīvortiī n.

noun, second declension

The divorce itself; “to divorce someone” is dīvortium facere cum aliquō (aliquā), as Cicero writes of Lentulus and Metella (Traupman 194 and Morgan–Owens give the same phrase). From dīvertere, to go different ways: the word also means a fork in a road, and dīvortium aquārum a watershed (Cic. Att. 5.20.3).

Other words

  • nūntium remittere (uxōrī) — to divorce (one’s wife), to send her notice of divorce

    also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 1.183; Att. 1.13.3 (Lewis & Short, s.v. nūntius)

    The act of divorcing, said by Cicero of a husband and also of a wife who leaves her husband (Top. 19). Nūntius here is the message, not the messenger.

  • repudium, repudiī n. — repudiation; the breaking off of a marriage or an engagement

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Plaut. Aul. 4.10.69; Ter. Phorm. 5.7.35: repudium remittere (Lewis & Short); Vulg. Mt. 5.31: libellum repudiī

    (the legal word; in comedy of breaking off a betrothal (Plaut., Ter.))

    The jurists distinguish it from dīvortium: an engagement can be broken off by repudium but not by dīvortium. Cicero uses only dīvortium (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Lentulum cum Metellā certē fēcisse dīvortium

    that Lentulus has certainly divorced MetellaCic. Att. 13.7.1 (Lewis & Short)

  • uxōrī sit reddunda dōs dīvortiō

    on divorce the dowry would have to be returned to the wifePlaut. Stich. 2.1.48 (Lewis & Short)

  • dīvortium facere cum aliquō

    to divorce someoneTraupman 194

  • dīvortium petere

    to seek a divorceTraupman 194

See also marriage, separate.
